extracted.intended_audience: practicing patent attorneys, judges, and advanced law students working on patent infringement (doctrine of equivalents and combination claims)
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluate whether accused devices infringe combination claims, focusing on the doctrine of equivalents, tests of equivalency (function and way), interchangeability, and how the scope of equivalents varies with the character of the invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Materiality of parts in combination claims
rubrics_metrics.description: The patentee makes all the parts of a combination material, when he claims them in combination and not separately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a claim recites elements only as a combination, each element is material to infringement analysis. This rule is subject to exceptions where patentability depends on a particular form; e.g., a shoe last made in two sections may infringe a patent for a last of same shape made in three sections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Result-oriented (means/result) claims coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: A patentee may claim so much of the described mechanism as produces a particular described result; such a claim is infringed by one who makes any apparatus comprising enough of the described devices to produce the specified result by the specified mode of operation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims drafted to produce a specified result can be infringed by assemblies that include sufficient described components to achieve that result, even if not identical in form to the patentee's embodiment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Union or separation of integral parts does not avoid infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: Infringement is not averred by uniting two elements of a machine or manufacture into one integral part, if the united part performs the same function in substantially the same way; nor by the separation of one integral part into two, the two parts doing substantially what was done by the single part.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Changes in physical structure (combining or splitting parts) will not avoid infringement where the functional performance and manner remain substantially the same; cases distinguish situations where a remaining element is made to do double work.

rubrics_metrics.name: No substitution of an equivalent avails to avert infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: No substitution of an equivalent for any ingredient of a combination covered by any claim of a patent can avert a charge of infringement of that claim, whether or not the equivalent is mentioned in the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Doctrine of equivalents may be invoked even if equivalents are neither claimed nor described. Conversely, substitution of something which is not an equivalent will avoid infringement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentee deemed to claim all forms copying the invention absent disclaimer
rubrics_metrics.description: The patentee, having described his invention and shown its principles, and claimed it in that form which most perfectly embodies it, is, in contemplation of law, deemed to claim every form in which his invention may be copied, unless he manifests an intention to disclaim some of these forms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This principle supports a broad application of equivalents, especially for combination patents; a clear disclaimer in the specification can limit coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specified material may preclude equivalence
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a patentee states in his specification that a particular part of his invention is to be constructed of a particular material, and states or implies that he does not contemplate any other material as being suitable for the purpose, it is not certain that any other material will be treated by a court as an equivalent of the one recommended.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Express limitation or endorsement of a specific material can reduce or eliminate equivalence for alternative materials (though courts have found equivalence in some cases, e.g., celluloid held equivalent to metal in a particular context).

rubrics_metrics.name: Equivalence requires performing the same function
rubrics_metrics.description: One thing, to be the equivalent of another, must perform the same functions as that other; if it performs the same function, the fact that it also performs another function is immaterial; but it cannot be such an equivalent if it does less.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identity of function is a necessary test: an accused device must respond fully to the claimed function(s). A device that also does extra work can still be an equivalent, but one that fails to perform the claimed function cannot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equivalence requires performing the function in substantially the same way
rubrics_metrics.description: Function must be performed in substantially the same way by an alleged equivalent as by the thing of which it is alleged to be an equivalent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This 'substantial sameness of way' is not strict identity of mechanism or theoretical scientific sameness; courts ask whether the practical manner of performing the function is substantially the same (examples: screw vs lever vs wedge; levers and springs as interchangeable in many arts).

rubrics_metrics.name: Function test is necessary but not sufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: The test of function (identity of function) is only the first of several tests of equivalency; the fact that one thing performs the same function though necessary is not sufficient to make it an equivalent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both identity of function and substantial identity of way must be met; other contextual considerations (e.g., prior art, environment) also bear on equivalence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equivalence is environment-dependent
rubrics_metrics.description: One thing may be an equivalent of another in one environment, and not such an equivalent in another situation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whether a substitute is an equivalent can change with operating conditions or environment (e.g., springs vs weights may be equivalents generally but not where a weight will not operate successfully). Courts examine the particular environment and functional fit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interchangeability/radical unfitness test
rubrics_metrics.description: Interchangeability usually requires change of form to fit the thing interchanged to its new environment; non-interchangeability involves such radical unfitness for a proposed position and function as cannot be removed by any change of form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a proposed substitute would require only reasonable form changes to perform the claimed function, interchangeability may support equivalence; but radical inability to function in the claimed position negates equivalence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equivalent need not have been known at time of invention
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a device, in order to be an equivalent of another, must have been known at the time of the invention — the question is answered in the negative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although once contested, weight of authority holds that later-developed substitutes can be equivalents; a narrow exception exists where patentee had tried and failed to use a material (one court held that later successful use by another could not be an equivalent).

rubrics_metrics.name: Range of equivalents corresponds with character and scope of invention
rubrics_metrics.description: The range of equivalents covered by the patent corresponds with the character of the invention, and includes all forms which embody the substance of the invention, and by like mechanical co-operation effect substantially the same result.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pioneer or primary inventions are generally entitled to a looser, broader range of equivalents; narrower (secondary) inventions receive a tighter range. The breadth of equivalents is calibrated to degree and character of the invention rather than a rigid primary/secondary dichotomy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-part test of equivalency and elasticity of 'substantial'
rubrics_metrics.description: There are two tests of equivalency: 1. Identity of function. 2. Substantial identity of way of performing that function. The second test is somewhat elastic because it contains the word 'substantial.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Elasticity of 'substantial' varies with the prior art: when extensive prior art narrows the invention, 'substantial' gives little elasticity; when fewer prior inventions preceded, 'substantial' allows more differences. Extremely useful or strictly primary inventions receive more generous application of 'substantial.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Presumption from grant of subsequent patent (limited)
rubrics_metrics.description: The grant of a subsequent patent raises a legal presumption of patentable difference from an earlier invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This presumption is not conclusive: a later patent may still embody things that are the exclusive property of an earlier patentee. Presumption is most applicable where the later patent is not merely an improvement on the earlier; courts interpret it in context (i.e., improvements-on-prior-art vs different species).
